title: Let's Talk About Text: Part 2 — Narrative Picture Books and Science Instruction
author: O'Mullins
summary: In this second installment of a series on text types, the author addresses a specific concern within knowledge-building curriculum: will moving to information-heavy science content squeeze out the beloved narrative picture books that elementary teachers have always used? The answer is no — but the article is precise about why, and about what role narrative picture books should and should not play in science instruction. Drawing on Neuman et al. (2026) research showing that preschoolers learned more about insects from informational text than from narrative text, the author argues narrative books should not be used to introduce or carry the primary load of new science content; doing so splits attention between narrative and concept in a way that disadvantages comprehension of both. Instead, narrative picture books are most powerful after foundational content is established — as a vehicle for vocabulary reinforcement, emotional engagement with science topics, and building the cross-curricular connections that deepen rather than introduce understanding. The article is practically grounded throughout, with specific examples of books that integrate elegantly with science units and guidance on when to deploy them.
points: Neuman et al. (2026) provides the empirical foundation: preschoolers learned more about insects from informational text than narrative text, because narrative creates cognitive load that competes with content learning when concepts are new.

Narrative picture books belong after foundational content is established, not before it: once students have the conceptual structure, narrative can reinforce vocabulary, build engagement, and deepen understanding without splitting attention between story and concept.

High-quality picture books always have a place in the elementary classroom, and knowledge-building curriculum does not eliminate them — it repositions them, from 'introduce this concept' to 'extend and enrich this concept already taught.'

Because elementary science connects to so many dimensions of daily life, many books that were never designed as science resources can be used to reinforce science vocabulary and concepts, expanding what counts as usable content without sacrificing narrative quality.

The cognitive load principle here is generalizable beyond science: any narrative text used to introduce new conceptual content faces the same split-attention problem, which is why sequencing content instruction before narrative engagement produces better retention of both.
